solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Almost lose sight of mischievous spirit (6)

indicatorNotes.Almost: What is almost there falls just short, so the last letter of the phrase is dropped.

blocks.note: Losing your sight is a two-word phrase, a verb of becoming plus sightless; its first word, the verb, is used whole.
The second word of that phrase, with its last letter cut off.

annotation.surface: Someone is bewitched by an impish sprite until they can barely see.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole phrase GO BLIND is what "lose sight" gives, and "Almost" trims only its final D.
annotation.definitionFit: A goblin is a small, mischievous creature of folklore.

entries.clue: It may well be read below stairs (3,5)

annotation.definition: It may well be read below stairs

blocks.note: the surface wants a book or letter; what is read here is a dial showing units used
the surface wants the servants' quarters; here it is the cupboard under the stairs, where British homes often keep the supply

annotation.surface: A book or letter is being read in the servants' quarters of a grand house.
annotation.walkthrough: "Below stairs" suggests servants reading, but meters are "read" by the gas company, and they are often kept under the stairs.
annotation.definitionFit: A gas meter is read to record usage and commonly sits in the cupboard under the stairs in British homes.

entries.clue: Like the toast that’s mostly spoken (8)

annotation.definition: Like the toast that’s mostly spoken

blocks.note: toast here is bread, not a speech: it describes how the slice is spread
all but the first letter of the answer is a word for spoken

annotation.surface: An after-dinner toast is mostly talk rather than drink.
annotation.walkthrough: Toast here is bread, not a speech; the joke is that BUTTERED, all but its first letter, is UTTERED, meaning spoken.
annotation.definitionFit: Buttered describes toast spread with butter, the usual way it is eaten.

entries.clue: Matter brought up in arithmetic (4)

indicatorNotes.brought up: In a down entry, what is brought up is read from the bottom upwards, so the letters run in reverse.
indicatorNotes.in: The answer sits in the next word, inside its run of letters.

blocks.note: Four letters sitting inside ariTHMETIc: M, E, T, I.

annotation.surface: A topic has been raised during a maths lesson.
annotation.walkthrough: "Brought up" looks like "raised for discussion", which suits "Matter", but in a down clue it means read upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: An item is a matter or point on a list or agenda.

entries.clue: Pre-war competition? (4,4)

blocks.note: the period of military build-up that precedes fighting
a contest between nations to out-arm each other, not a sporting event

annotation.surface: A sporting contest held in the years before a war.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: the competition is between nations stockpiling weapons, which often comes before war.
annotation.definitionFit: An arms race is a contest between countries to build up weapons.

entries.clue: Record of ex-officers, the retiring sort, it seems (8,4)

blocks.note: the naval register of retired officers liable to recall
read literally: a list of the reserved, that is, the shy

annotation.surface: A register of former officers turns out to be full of shy types.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half reads the phrase literally: a list of the reserved, that is, the retiring or shy.
annotation.definitionFit: The reserved list is the register of retired naval officers who can be recalled.

entries.clue: Such a night leads to serious trouble – and gaol! (4)

indicatorNotes.leads to: The leads of words are their first letters, taken from the words that follow.

blocks.note: First letters of Serious, Trouble, And, Gaol.

annotation.surface: A wild night out ends with arrests and a spell in jail.
annotation.walkthrough: A stag night is the British name for a groom's party before his wedding, notorious for ending in trouble.
annotation.definitionFit: Stag is the British adjective for an all-male party before a wedding, so "such a night" is a stag night.

entries.clue: Sharp spies about to ensnare detectives (6)

indicatorNotes.about: About means turned round, so the spies' letters are written backwards.
indicatorNotes.to ensnare: What ensnares something traps it inside, so the detectives go within.

blocks.note: The CIA is the US spy agency.
CID, the Criminal Investigation Department, is the British police detective branch.

annotation.surface: Some sharp-witted agents circle round to trap police detectives.
annotation.walkthrough: "Sharp" looks like it describes the spies, but it is the definition, standing apart at the front.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of taste: acids taste sour, so something acidic is sharp.

entries.clue: Being like a bird in east New York (6)

indicatorNotes.in: The bird goes in, placed inside the letters for New York.

blocks.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east.
NY is the standard abbreviation for New York.
The tit is a small garden bird.

annotation.surface: Someone feels like a bird trapped in the eastern side of New York.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the noun: a being, not the verb "being".
annotation.definitionFit: An entity is a being, something that exists in its own right.

entries.clue: Man’s best friend, maybe, created this! (6)

blocks.note: a dog, here a gundog breed
the person who made this crossword

annotation.surface: A dog lover boasts that the family pet invented something.
annotation.walkthrough: "This" is the crossword itself, and the person who creates one is its setter; the other setter is a gundog.
annotation.definitionFit: A setter is a breed of dog, and a crossword's author is its setter.

entries.clue: Attempt is first of thousands for Montaigne, say (8)

indicatorNotes.first of: Only the first letter of the next word is taken.

blocks.note: To essay is to attempt; an essay is also an attempt.
Used as it stands.
First letter of thousands.

annotation.surface: A remark that Montaigne began by writing thousands of trial pieces.
annotation.walkthrough: Montaigne, the 16th-century French writer, invented the essay form; "say" marks him as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Montaigne founded the essay as a form.

entries.clue: Shine, bilingually (6,6)

blocks.note: a glossy finish for wood
two languages named side by side, one from France and one from Poland

annotation.surface: A word for gleam, given in two languages.
annotation.walkthrough: "Bilingually" hints at two languages, French and Polish, which together name the high-gloss wood finish.
annotation.definitionFit: French polish is a shellac finish that gives furniture a deep shine.

entries.clue: Garden shed enthusiasts have the prototype (4)

indicatorNotes.have: The words have the answer, holding it within their letters.

blocks.note: Inside shED ENthusiasts.

annotation.surface: Hobbyists who love garden sheds own the original model.
annotation.walkthrough: Eden is the prototype garden, the first one in Genesis, so "the prototype" sharpens the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Eden was the first garden, the model for all others.

entries.clue: Faithful argue endlessly in cathedral city (5)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: Without their ends, so the last letter of each word goes.

blocks.note: TRUE with its last letter cut.
ROW, to argue, with its last letter cut.

annotation.surface: Loyal churchgoers keep squabbling in a cathedral city.
annotation.walkthrough: "Endlessly" applies to both words. Row, rhyming with cow, is a British word for a quarrel.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Truro, in Cornwall, has a Victorian cathedral and city status.

entries.clue: Colour can, with time (4)

blocks.note: A tin is a can.
T is the abbreviation for time.

annotation.surface: An instruction that a can of paint will change colour over time.
annotation.walkthrough: "Colour" is the definition, not a verb acting on "can".
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a tint is a shade or hue.

entries.clue: Men in food riot are united (2,3,4)

indicatorNotes.riot: A riot is disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new order.

blocks.note: The letters to rearrange.

annotation.surface: Hungry men rioting over food show solidarity.
annotation.walkthrough: "In" looks like a placement word but is part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: people who share an opinion are said to be of one mind.

entries.clue: Girl donating heart and liver, for example (5)

indicatorNotes.donating heart: Giving away her heart, the word loses its middle letters.

blocks.note: GIRL with its heart, IR, removed.
Used as it stands.

annotation.surface: A young woman is an organ donor, giving her heart and her liver.
annotation.walkthrough: The organ-donation surface makes "heart" and "liver" look like a pair; only the liver is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the liver secretes bile, which makes it a gland.

entries.clue: Easy passage for a camel, apparently (3,2,1,6)

annotation.definition: Easy passage for a camel, apparently

blocks.note: the surface pictures a smooth desert route; the setter means a tiny opening
points to the Gospel saying that a camel passes through it more easily than a rich man enters heaven

annotation.surface: A route that a camel finds simple to travel.
annotation.walkthrough: Jesus said it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter heaven; "apparently" nods to that saying.
annotation.definitionFit: A proverbial image from the Gospels, where the tiny needle opening is paradoxically easier for a camel than heaven for the rich.

entries.clue: Black Prince turns out smarter (8)

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils.
Prince Rainier III ruled Monaco.

annotation.surface: The Black Prince, Edward III's son, proves to be the cleverer one.
annotation.walkthrough: "Black Prince" reads as Edward of Woodstock, but it splits into B and a different prince, Rainier of Monaco.
annotation.definitionFit: Brainier means more intelligent, that is smarter.

entries.clue: Blotches skins develop, injecting drug (8)

indicatorNotes.develop: To develop is to change form, so the letters are rearranged.
indicatorNotes.injecting: Injecting puts one thing inside another, so the drug goes within.

blocks.note: The letters of SKINS rearranged.
Pot is slang for cannabis.

annotation.surface: Skin blemishes appear after someone injects a drug.
annotation.walkthrough: The medical surface makes "Blotches" look like skin marks, but they are ink stains.
annotation.definitionFit: Blots of spilt ink are called inkspots, the stains the definition names.

entries.clue: Where steeplechasers go, sooner or later (2,3,4,3)

blocks.note: the long race over fences they are running
eventually

annotation.surface: Steeplechase runners will get where they are going eventually.
annotation.walkthrough: A steeplechase is a long race over obstacles, so its runners are literally in the long run.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom meaning eventually, and literally the long race steeplechasers run.

entries.clue: Authorise advice for hair treatment (6)

blocks.note: to allow
split in two, it is an instruction to give the hair a perm

annotation.surface: A salon needs official approval before giving advice on hair.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half splits the answer: PERM IT is the advice to give the hair a perm.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym, allow, while the split reading gives an instruction to a hairdresser.

entries.clue: Jump like a big cat, under pressure (6)

indicatorNotes.under: In a down entry, what is under comes lower down, so the cat follows the P.

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for pressure.
The ounce is another name for the snow leopard.

annotation.surface: A big cat leaps when it is under pressure.
annotation.walkthrough: The ounce is a lesser-known name for the snow leopard, and it also looks like a weight, not a cat.
annotation.definitionFit: To pounce is to jump suddenly, as a cat does on prey.

entries.clue: Oral taken in college (4)

indicatorNotes.Oral: Oral means by mouth, so what follows is heard rather than read.

blocks.note: Food taken in has been swallowed; that past participle, spoken, fits the letters wanted.

annotation.surface: A spoken exam is sat at a college.
annotation.walkthrough: "Oral" looks like a noun for an exam, but it is the signal word; "taken in" means swallowed.
annotation.definitionFit: Eton College is the famous English public school.

entries.clue: Does highest in pecking order rule it? (5)

annotation.definition: Does highest in pecking order rule it?

blocks.note: the cockerel, top of the farmyard hierarchy
the idiom for being in charge names the place hens perch

annotation.surface: A question about whether the top ranked in a hierarchy is in charge.
annotation.walkthrough: The top of the pecking order among hens is the rooster, who proverbially rules the roost.
annotation.definitionFit: A roost is where birds settle, and to rule the roost is to be in charge.

entries.clue: What some doctors do in return for little drinks (4)

indicatorNotes.in return: In return means going back, so the word is written backwards.

blocks.note: Spin doctors spin: they put a favourable slant on news.

annotation.surface: Doctors accept small drinks as payment.
annotation.walkthrough: "Doctors" suggests medicine, but spin doctors are political press officers.
annotation.definitionFit: A nip is a small drink of spirits.

entries.clue: See 15
Pocket item, one with rotating ball, appropriately (4)

indicatorNotes.rotating: Rotating turns the ball round, so its letters run backwards.
indicatorNotes.with: The one is held with the ball, inside it.

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one.
An orb is a ball.

annotation.surface: A pen in the pocket has a turning ball at its tip.
annotation.walkthrough: A Biro, British for a ballpoint pen, works by a rotating ball, which is why the wordplay is "appropriate".
annotation.definitionFit: A Biro is a ballpoint pen, commonly carried in a pocket.

entries.clue: Little chap reportedly mad to joinin (8)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: What is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the answer is what the phrase is heard as.

blocks.note: Mad gives an adjective for frenzied, which is joined to IN and the pair spoken as one word.

annotation.surface: A small man is said to be crazy to join in.
annotation.walkthrough: The scraped clue runs "join in" together; the wordplay is MANIC joined to IN.
annotation.definitionFit: A diminutive: the -kin suffix means small, so a mannikin is a tiny man.

entries.clue: After fifty I offer love . . . . and lust! (6)

indicatorNotes.After: The rest is placed after the fifty.

blocks.note: L is the Roman numeral fifty.
Used as it stands.
A bid is an offer.
Love is zero in tennis, O.

annotation.surface: Someone past fifty offers love and admits to lust.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fifty" reads as an age, which is the joke of the surface; it is the Roman numeral.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: libido is sexual drive.

entries.clue: A brother’s dated plays appear on stage (5,3,6)

indicatorNotes.plays: Letters that play move about freely, so they are rearranged.

blocks.note: The letters to rearrange.

annotation.surface: A sibling's old-fashioned plays are finally staged.
annotation.walkthrough: "Plays" looks like the theatre noun that suits the surface, but it is the verb telling the letters to move.
annotation.definitionFit: A theatre idiom: the boards are the stage floor, so treading them means acting.

entries.clue: See 30
